generatedProse.concept-context: Whatever you are studying, critical reading is what turns AI output into something you can safely use. Treat every answer in your subject as a draft to test, not a fact to accept. Check its claims against your sources, confirm anything it cites, and ask what a confident, tidy answer has quietly left out.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two psychology students who ask a chatbot to summarise the evidence on a contested question for a psychology essay.

{{learner-a}} gets a fluent summary with a striking statistic and three named studies. It reads as though an expert wrote it, so {{learner-a}} builds the essay around the figure and cites the studies. The statistic was invented, one study does not exist, and only one side of the debate appears. Nothing was checked, and the essay rests on things that were never true.

{{learner-b}} gets a similar summary and treats it as a set of leads, not facts. {{learner-b}} tries to verify the statistic and cannot find it, checks each study in the library, and notices a major counter-argument is missing. {{learner-b}} keeps what holds up, drops the rest, and reads more widely to fill the gap.

Both got the same confident answer. Only {{learner-b}} read it critically, and so caught the invented figure, the false source and the missing side.
generatedProse.summary: Critical evaluation is the single most important skill in learning with AI. You fact-check the content, verify every source, ask whose view the answer reflects, and notice what it leaves out, treating a confident tone as no proof of accuracy. You can now evaluate an AI answer, recognise the failure patterns that should make you suspicious, and bring steady checking habits to your own work. Next the course names the specific ways AI output goes wrong.

check.body: A chatbot gives you a confident claim and a source to support a point in {{context}}. What should you do before using them?

items.text: Fact-check the claim against a source you trust, and look up the source to confirm it exists.
Use them, because the source is named and the claim is specific.
Use them, because the answer is detailed and confidently written.
Use them, as long as they fit the argument you want to make in {{context}}.

feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, you fact-check the claim and confirm the source before relying on either.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. A named source, a confident tone and a convenient fit are not proof that a claim or a source is real.
feedback.incorrectFinal: You fact-check the claim against a trusted source and look up the source to confirm it exists. A specific claim, a confident tone and a convenient fit prove nothing.
